taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes disjunct southern California and Sierra San Pedro Martir populations were treated as a distinct species by Grismer (2002).
fieldMarks: Small (up to about 15 cm total length), gray to brown, usually with blotches or crossbars and a pale dorsolateral stripe on each side.
Scales small, slightly rough with short spines; no distinct blue patches on the throat sides (throat may be blue-mottled).
Males: dark blue patch on each side of the belly and blue-mottled or streaked throat; females whitish below with faint or absent blue.
Versus western fence lizard: smaller, less prickly scales, no yellow on the back of the thighs, and pale stripes rather than a checkered pattern.
behavior: Ground dweller that perches on rocks, logs and snags; uses rodent burrows, shrubs and logs for cover.
Active about March-April to September-October; inactive in cold winter weather.
Eats beetles, flies, ants, caterpillars, spiders, ticks and mites.
Eggs laid May-July; most adult females in Colorado and Utah produce two clutches a year.
habitat: Sagebrush and other shrublands (manzanita, ceanothus), pinyon-juniper and open ponderosa pine or Douglas-fir woodland.
Needs open ground with some low bushes.
range: Washington, Idaho, Montana and North Dakota south to northern Baja California, northern Arizona and northwestern New Mexico, east into western Nebraska; about 150-3,200 m. Not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Western fence lizard
lookalikes.howToTell: Larger, prickly scales with longer spines, yellow or orange on the rear of the thighs, and a checkered or V-shaped pattern.
